title: Derek Welton a different man off drugs
article: A coroner's inquest into the death of Derek Welton has examined Welton's trouble with drugs, his mental instability and his run-ins with police.
But on Wednesday, the inquest's presiding coroner and jury heard about who Welton was at his best.
"He was an amazing person," said friend Corey Orcutt.
"He was always happy, always in a good mood, always willing to help."
Welton was shot and killed by police on March 1, 2009.
No criminal charges have been recommended against the officers involved in the incident.
The coroner's inquest, meanwhile, began on Monday and offers a four-man, three-woman jury the opportunity to make recommendations that could prevent deaths in similar situations in the future.
Welton, the inquest revealed, had been taking drugs and was acting irrationally when local RCMP arrived at his door the evening of his death.
Orcutt said that when Welton was using drugs, he could become "scary.
But he also said Welton was a happy-go-lucky kind of person who'd bend over backward for his friends.
Orcutt -- who is now drug-free -- explained he and Welton and met about a year and a half before at an Alcoholics Anonymous meeting.
The two had a couple of relapses together but would then attempt to get clean. They had a good friendship and hung out often. Both rode motorcycles, and their girlfriends were friends.
Orcutt also told the inquest about the day Welton was killed. He'd been at Welton's trailer where the two men smoked a gram or two of crack cocaine for a couple hours.
Orcutt made it clear that Welton was a good person, and any bad behaviour was caused by drug use.
"When Derek used, he would change," Orcutt explained.
"That was the effect of the drugs on him."
Meanwhile, Welton's father, Carroll, hopes the inquest will save future lives.
"I hope this helps somebody else," he said outside the Duncan Law Courts Wednesday afternoon.
"I think there's always an opportunity for doing things better," he added, saying perhaps his son could have been talked down with help from psychiatric staff on scene to help police.
He didn't appear to have criticism for the RCMP.
"The police had a hard job to do," he said.
During the inquest, Carroll Welton explained his wife died when Derek was 14, and he believes his son suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder afterward.
"It was a devastating thing to him," his father said, explaining Derek was "just like a zombie for awhile" after her death.
"They were very close."
Welton died after police officers responded to an abandoned 911 call with the intention of transporting Welton to the hospital for medical treatment under the Mental Health Act.
Const. Kara Gelech had deployed her Taser in an attempt to stun Welton so police could apprehend him.
Instead, Welton attacked the officers inside his trailer with knives. It took two bullets and another hit with the Taser to subdue Welton and get him to the hospital, where was pronounced dead.
The seven-member inquest jury was sequestered Thursday morning, tasked with making recommendations to assist in preventing similar situations.
